entities.name: Hagnon of Tarsus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Hagnon of Tarsus, an ancient Greek rhetorician and Academic Skeptic philosopher active in the 2nd century BCE, stands as a notable figure in the intellectual currents of the Hellenistic period, particularly for his provocative challenge to the foundational status of rhetoric. As a pupil of Carneades, the head of the New Academy in Athens, Hagnon inherited and applied the rigorous skeptical methodology to disciplines beyond pure philosophy, extending it to the very art of persuasion that underpinned much of public life and education in the Greco-Roman world. His significance lies in representing a radical fringe within the skeptical tradition, pushing its anti-dogmatic stance to question the methodological basis of established arts.

His most celebrated, or perhaps notorious, work was *Rhetorices accusatio* ('Accusation of Rhetoric'), a treatise in which he vehemently argued that rhetoric was not an art (τέχνη). This denial was not merely semantic; it attacked the systematic, teachable, and principled nature that ancient theorists like Aristotle and Isocrates had painstakingly ascribed to rhetoric. Hagnon's argument likely rested on the Academic Skeptic premise that no certain knowledge or definitive rules could be established, thereby undermining the very possibility of a 'techne' based on such principles. His criticisms were part of a broader philosophical debate on the nature of knowledge, skill, and their application in practical fields.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Hagnon of Tarsus, through his radical critique of rhetoric, significantly contributed to a vigorous intellectual debate that shaped the theoretical defenses of rhetoric by later Roman authors like Quintilian. His work highlights the critical spirit of Academic Skepticism applied to practical arts in the Hellenistic world.
